input.query: Compare metric-learning approaches for few-shot image classification.
input.survey:
# Metric Learning for Few-Shot Image Classification: An Embedding, Class-Representation, and Similarity Comparison Review

## Abstract

Metric-learning few-shot classifiers learn embeddings and comparison rules on base classes, then predict novel queries from relations to scarce support examples. This review compares them by three organizing stages: feature embedding, class representation, and distance or similarity. Matching Networks use support instances; prototypes summarize classes as points; Relation Networks learn nonlinear scores; later methods add query conditioning, distributions, asymmetric measures, subspaces, region comparisons, multi-stage features, and task adaptation. Embedding losses such as K-tuplet, Proto-Triplet, and ICNN shape feature geometry, while richer class models express uncertainty or variation. Reported gains—including ADM's 3.02% and 1.56% 5-way 1-shot gains on miniImageNet and tieredImageNet—remain tied to each paper's benchmark, backbone, shots, source data, and protocol. Evidence therefore supports localized comparisons, not a universal ranking: same-domain miniImageNet tests differ from cross-dataset transfer, CUB fine-grained results, flexible-way or multi-source tasks, VTAB plus Meta-Dataset family comparisons, and specialized SAR evidence. Direct ranking requires matched backbones, data scale, episodes, adaptation rules, and evaluation protocols. [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:abstract:0:94ff5952b4c1:claim:75c753f3205c] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:abstract:1:672489eb0fa9:claim:b75d4ecca446] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:421a9600bb91] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:abstract:claim:92863cf84848] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_few_shot_deep_metric_learning_methods:0:c53378070ee7:claim:65f78a914028] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:41e8ea8f67cc] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:introduction:3:fb29f917e0e2:claim:61402de0d456] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:1:f6a11fe47f73:claim:852780aa640e] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:abstract:claim:823c76c237f3] [E:arxiv:1711.06025:abstract:claim:1a5f717da016] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:2:4c9f8b613811:claim:6ec2ea7e56e2] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:2:4c9f8b613811:claim:5c1b3aa35115] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:abstract:claim:24974efbef21] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:abstract:claim:1b369d5d7d5f] [E:arxiv:2002.00153:abstract:claim:68151909197b] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:8a4c1729167e] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:02380d44985c] [E:arxiv:2409.07989:abstract:claim:baa36cba9b0a] [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:3b48d1371831] [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:f090d17c92ce] [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:c7b491e4de94] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:3:11bb8b6bf73e:claim:b3038684f21d] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:introduction:3:fb29f917e0e2:claim:899fa0448e5a] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:introduction:3:fb29f917e0e2:claim:9f8299b19a8c] [E:arxiv:2104.02638:abstract:claim:727abcd8e3b1] [E:arxiv:2104.02638:abstract:claim:1ad165a11aa4] [E:arxiv:2104.02638:section:abstract:2:baccf9bc87dd:claim:76401b33d078] [E:arxiv:2104.02638:section:abstract:2:baccf9bc87dd:claim:ecf4ad2d5e3a] [E:arxiv:2306.09592:abstract:claim:a84f557f7113] [E:arxiv:1802.04376:section:abstract:4:8531e2861789:claim:b08bca94e51c]

## Introduction

Few-shot image classification asks a model to recognize query images from classes represented by only a few labeled support examples. The central difficulty is that ordinary supervised training or fine-tuning can overfit when each novel class has very few samples. Metric-learning approaches address this by learning a transferable embedding and/or similarity measure on base classes, then classifying novel query images according to their relations to support examples or class representations in that learned space. [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:abstract:0:94ff5952b4c1:claim:75c753f3205c] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:abstract:1:672489eb0fa9:claim:b75d4ecca446] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:421a9600bb91]

This review compares metric-learning methods by the stage at which they introduce inductive bias: how image features are embedded, how scarce support examples are summarized into a class representation, and how query-to-class similarity or distance is computed. That three-stage organization follows the review grouping of feature-embedding learning, class-representation learning, and distance/similarity-measure learning; it is an organizing lens for this comparison, not a universal taxonomy or a claim that every paper uses the same labels. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:abstract:claim:92863cf84848] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_few_shot_deep_metric_learning_methods:0:c53378070ee7:claim:65f78a914028] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:41e8ea8f67cc]

The common operational setting is episodic N-way k-shot classification: an episode contains a support set with k labeled examples per N class and a query set whose labels are predicted. Methods such as Matching Networks, Prototypical Networks, and Relation Networks instantiate different choices within this framework, respectively emphasizing nearest-example comparison, class prototypes, and learned relation scores. Later methods extend these ideas with task-aware embeddings, local or distributional representations, subspace models, and auxiliary metric losses. [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:introduction:3:fb29f917e0e2:claim:61402de0d456] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:1:f6a11fe47f73:claim:852780aa640e] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:abstract:claim:823c76c237f3]

The scope is limited to image classification and to approaches whose prediction rule is fundamentally based on learned relations between queries and support classes, even when they are trained episodically or combined with meta-learning. Optimization-based meta-learners that primarily learn parameter updates, large-scale transfer methods, zero-shot semantic-attribute models, and domain-specific SAR benchmarks are treated only as boundaries or evaluation context; they are not relabeled as metric-learning methods. Cross-family results also cannot be ranked directly unless backbones, training data, episodes, and evaluation protocols match. [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:3b48d1371831] [E:arxiv:2104.02638:abstract:claim:727abcd8e3b1] [E:arxiv:1607.08085:abstract:claim:9a9f1e6883c5] [E:arxiv:2104.02638:section:abstract:1:f6c575ccd9aa:claim:6dc5641724f0] [E:arxiv:2306.09592:abstract:claim:a84f557f7113]

## Background and Method Taxonomy

The taxonomy used in this review groups metric-learning methods by where their main modeling choice acts: feature embedding, class representation, and distance or similarity measure. The feature-embedding stage maps support and query images into a shared representation; the class-representation stage decides whether each class is represented by individual examples, a point prototype, a distribution, or a subspace; and the comparison stage applies an analytic measure or a learned network to score a query against each class. This is the review's organizing choice for comparing methods, not a universal partition or a claim that individual algorithms belong to only one stage. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:abstract:claim:92863cf84848] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_few_shot_deep_metric_learning_methods:0:c53378070ee7:claim:65f78a914028] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:41e8ea8f67cc] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:abstract:1:672489eb0fa9:claim:b75d4ecca446]

At the first level, embedding-focused methods differ in whether they seek one task-agnostic embedding or adapt the representation to the episode. A task-agnostic encoder is trained so that the same feature space transfers across episodes, whereas task-specific or task-aware methods transform or select features using the support context, query context, or both. The review literature also lists embedding improvements based on data augmentation, multi-task learning, self-supervision, and semi-supervised signals; these are training or representation strategies, not separate prediction rules by themselves. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_few_shot_deep_metric_learning_methods:0:c53378070ee7:claim:65f78a914028] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:421a9600bb91]

At the class-representation level, nearest-example or instance-to-instance methods compare a query directly with support images. Prototype methods instead summarize each class with a reference vector, commonly by averaging support embeddings or by learning a weighted prototype. Distributional and subspace models move beyond a single point: they represent uncertainty, spatial structure, feature diversity, or a class-specific manifold, and then compare the query with that richer object. These choices matter because one or five support images may be noisy or insufficient to estimate a class center reliably. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:41e8ea8f67cc] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:8a4c1729167e] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:421a9600bb91]

At the comparison level, fixed analytical metrics and learned similarity functions form the main distinction. Fixed metrics include cosine or Euclidean-style distances and nearest-subspace distances; learned comparators use neural modules to output relation scores, allowing nonlinear, context-dependent comparisons. A further distinction is symmetry: conventional distances treat the two sides symmetrically, while some few-shot models argue that a query image and a support class are naturally asymmetric objects and therefore design asymmetric distribution measures. These are comparison criteria, not evidence that one form is universally better. [E:arxiv:2002.00153:abstract:claim:68151909197b] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:1:f6a11fe47f73:claim:852780aa640e] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:8a4c1729167e] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:421a9600bb91]

Metric learning overlaps with, but is not identical to, meta-learning and transfer learning. Episodic metric-learning methods commonly use a meta-learning training protocol: many sampled support-and-query tasks make training resemble the test task. However, meta-learning also includes optimization-based methods that primarily learn initialization or parameter-update rules, and transfer-learning methods typically pretrain a representation on large upstream data before adapting downstream. The cited review notes that these families can be combined, so a method can be metric-based in its prediction rule and meta-trained in its optimization procedure. [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:introduction:3:fb29f917e0e2:claim:61402de0d456] [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:3b48d1371831] [E:arxiv:2104.02638:section:abstract:1:f6c575ccd9aa:claim:6dc5641724f0] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:abstract:1:672489eb0fa9:claim:b75d4ecca446]

Several nearby objectives should be kept separate when interpreting comparisons. Zero-shot metric learning uses semantic attributes or other side information rather than a few labeled support images; adaptive metric learning for diverse language tasks addresses task variation outside the image-classification scope; and domain-specific SAR or cross-domain studies change the data distribution and benchmark. Likewise, interpretability, multi-level feature extraction, runtime, and cross-domain robustness are evaluation dimensions, not replacements for the embedding, class-representation, and comparison taxonomy. Results from these settings should not be merged into a single ranking unless the task, backbone, training data, and episodic protocol are matched. [E:arxiv:1607.08085:abstract:claim:9a9f1e6883c5] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:abstract:0:94ff5952b4c1:claim:75c753f3205c] [E:arxiv:1805.07513:abstract:claim:8090ccd62bec] [E:arxiv:2409.07989:abstract:claim:baa36cba9b0a] [E:arxiv:2306.09592:abstract:claim:a84f557f7113]

## Representative Methods

Instance-comparison methods form the simplest end of the metric-learning family. Matching Networks, as described in the K-tuplet paper, use an episodically trained embedding and an end-to-end k-nearest-neighbor-style prediction rule over support examples. Their main contribution is to make training resemble the support-to-query comparison performed at test time, but their applicability boundary is that the class is represented only by the available support instances; with one or noisy examples, there is no explicit mechanism for estimating a more stable class distribution. [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:1:f6a11fe47f73:claim:852780aa640e] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:41e8ea8f67cc] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:abstract:claim:823c76c237f3]

Prototypical methods move the modeling choice from raw nearest-neighbor comparison to a class-level point representation. The review describes prototypes as reference vectors for a class, commonly obtained by a simple or weighted average of support embeddings, or learned end-to-end. This reduces variance relative to comparing against individual examples and keeps the decision rule easy to interpret, usually by assigning a query to the nearest prototype. Its boundary is that a single vector can collapse within-class variation and may be sensitive to outliers or atypical support images. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:41e8ea8f67cc] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:421a9600bb91]

Relation Networks replace a fixed Euclidean or cosine comparison with a learned comparator. The method embeds query and support information, concatenates or otherwise presents query-class pairs to a relation module, and trains the module end-to-end to output a relation score; at test time it scores a query against each new class without updating the network for that episode. The contribution is flexibility: a nonlinear comparator can learn relationships that a fixed linear distance cannot express. The boundary is that this flexibility adds comparator parameters and learning burden, and a learned score does not by itself solve weak support-class representations. [E:arxiv:1711.06025:abstract:claim:1a5f717da016] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:1:f6a11fe47f73:claim:852780aa640e] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:abstract:claim:823c76c237f3]

The target-conditioned classifier paper makes class representation episode- and query-dependent rather than treating a prototype as fixed for all queries. Its architecture conditions class representations on the target image and trains a network to compare classes, allowing the comparator to emphasize class aspects relevant to the query. It reports strong performance on the Caltech-UCSD Birds fine-grained task, which is a useful applicability signal: query-conditioned comparison may help when subtle part or appearance cues distinguish similar classes. It should not be read as evidence that conditioning is universally superior across domains, because the cited evidence is tied to that fine-grained benchmark and the paper's experimental setting. [E:arxiv:1802.04376:section:abstract:4:8531e2861789:claim:b08bca94e51c] [E:arxiv:1802.04376:abstract:claim:dfbfdad30c36]

Embedding-focused metric learning argues that stronger feature geometry can improve even simple downstream comparisons. The deep K-tuplet Network extends triplet learning so that an anchor is compared jointly with multiple negative samples in an update rather than only one negative, aligning training more closely with N-way few-shot decisions. It also uses semi-hard mining to select informative triplets, with the stated goals of faster convergence and more stable training. The method can be combined with a learnable nonlinear distance, so its primary contribution is a more discriminative, transferable embedding rather than a new class-summary object. [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:2:4c9f8b613811:claim:6ec2ea7e56e2] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:2:4c9f8b613811:claim:5c1b3aa35115] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:abstract:claim:823c76c237f3] The evidence for K-tuplet learning covers both in-domain and cross-domain evaluation, but under the method's own protocol. The authors train on miniImageNet, test on miniImageNet novel classes, and also evaluate a model trained on miniImageNet on Caltech-101, CUB-200, Stanford Dogs, and Stanford Cars to assess cross-dataset generalization. They report that the method outperforms other metric-based approaches on miniImageNet and prior methods in the cross-dataset setting. These results support the claim that embedding geometry matters for transfer to unseen classes and datasets; they do not establish superiority over methods trained with different backbones, data scales, or adaptation protocols. [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:3:11bb8b6bf73e:claim:b3038684f21d] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:2:4c9f8b613811:claim:5c1b3aa35115] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:abstract:claim:823c76c237f3]

Proto-Triplet and ICNN losses are later embedding-geometry methods that act through optimization rather than through a new nearest-neighbor rule. Proto-Triplet adapts triplet loss to few-shot episodes by considering class prototypes and the relative intra-class and inter-class distances, while ICNN uses an inter- and intra-class nearest-neighbor score to assess and improve the separability of the learned latent space. The authors report about a 2% accuracy improvement over compared metric-based methods on miniImageNet and competitive generalization to Caltech, CUB, Dogs, and Cars. The boundary is that these are loss-level contributions: they can improve an embedding network but do not remove uncertainty about class representation or comparator design. [E:arxiv:2305.09062:abstract:claim:24974efbef21] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:abstract:claim:1b369d5d7d5f]

Distributional and asymmetric measures address a mismatch between point prototypes and the object being classified. The ADM paper argues that image-level features poorly estimate a class distribution when support samples are scarce, while symmetric instance-level metrics also ignore the natural directionality from a query image to a support class. ADM therefore represents queries and classes as multivariate local distributions and computes a joint local-and-global asymmetric measure between them; its contrastive measure strategy further shapes the comparison. This mechanism is most directly applicable when local descriptors and class-level distributions carry information that a global vector prototype loses. [E:arxiv:2002.00153:abstract:claim:68151909197b]

Subspace methods replace the class point with a geometric set capable of expressing variation. The subspace representation learning framework represents an image by a subspace in local CNN feature space and measures image-to-image similarity with weighted subspace distance. For K-shot classes, it aggregates support information through prototypical or discriminative template subspaces, extending vector-based metric learning to subspace representations. The authors' rationale is that subspaces preserve spatial structure and within-image diversity better than a global vector. The method is therefore a class-representation and comparison design, not merely a larger encoder; its trade-off is that estimating a meaningful subspace depends on having sufficient local feature structure and support variation. [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:8a4c1729167e] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:02380d44985c] Deep Subspace Network is a related subspace approach described in the review: each class is represented by a low-dimensional subspace constructed from support samples through singular value decomposition, and a query is assigned by a nearest-subspace classifier based on the distance between the query and its projection onto each class subspace. The review presents this model as more robust to noise and outliers than Prototypical Networks. That robustness claim should be attached to the cited review's characterization and the nearest-subspace mechanism; it does not imply that subspace models dominate prototype models on every dataset or backbone. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:421a9600bb91]

Variational distributional methods retain uncertainty instead of committing to one deterministic class center. The review describes a variational Bayesian few-shot framework that estimates each class distribution with a neural network and uses Kullback-Leibler divergence to measure sample-to-class relations, producing confidence for class assignment. This is appropriate when support scarcity makes point estimates unreliable, but it introduces distributional assumptions and an inference model that simple nearest-prototype methods do not require. Thus it occupies the class-distribution branch of the taxonomy, distinct from neural similarity scoring. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:421a9600bb91]

Region Comparison Network adds an interpretability-oriented local comparison mechanism. RCN learns regions that correspond between query and support images and uses these region-level relations to support few-shot decisions; Region Activation Mapping visualizes intermediate variables, and the method also generalizes task-level interpretability toward category-level prototypical parts. Its contribution is therefore both a local relational metric and a way to inspect which image regions influence the prediction. The applicability boundary is that visualization and prototypical-part extraction can explain a model's learned comparisons but do not themselves guarantee causal correctness or higher accuracy across unrelated tasks. [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:introduction:3:fb29f917e0e2:claim:899fa0448e5a] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:introduction:3:fb29f917e0e2:claim:9f8299b19a8c] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:abstract:0:94ff5952b4c1:claim:75c753f3205c]

Multi-stage embedding methods target information lost when a single distance is computed from one final feature vector. The cited MSENet approach uses a multi-output embedding network that extracts features from multiple stages so that shallow, detailed cues and deeper, abstract cues occupy distinct feature spaces; self-attention refines each stage, and learnable weights combine stage contributions. It is evaluated on miniImageNet and FC100 in 5-way 1-shot and 5-way 5-shot settings and on cross-domain tasks across eight datasets. Its evidence supports multi-level representation as an embedding enhancement, while its boundary is that added stages, attention, and stage weighting increase architectural complexity and must be compared under matched training conditions. [E:arxiv:2409.07989:abstract:claim:baa36cba9b0a]

Task-adaptive metrics address the assumption that one metric is appropriate for every episode. Meta-Metric-Learner combines a task-specific metric-based base learner with a meta-learner that specifies the base model, motivated by two complementary limitations: metric learning can accommodate varying numbers of classes but may fail when tasks require different metrics across domains, whereas optimization-based meta-learning can specify task models but often assumes homogeneous task structure. The method targets flexible class counts and more general cross-task metrics. Its evidence includes standard k-shot N-way tests and a realistic flexible-class-number setting in single-source and multi-source forms, so it should be understood as a hybrid metric-and-meta-learning approach rather than a pure fixed-metric classifier. [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:3b48d1371831] [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:f090d17c92ce] [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:c7b491e4de94]

The adaptive metric idea also appears outside natural images, which helps define the mechanism's boundary. In diverse natural-language tasks, a single metric is described as insufficient because task variation is high; the proposed adaptive approach selects a weighted combination of metrics obtained from meta-training tasks for a new task. That evidence supports the general principle of task-dependent metric selection, but it is not image-classification evidence and should not be used to rank vision models. It does clarify why a task-invariant metric can be restrictive when source tasks are heterogeneous. [E:arxiv:1805.07513:abstract:claim:8090ccd62bec]

Cross-domain metric learning makes the domain-shift limitation explicit. The study motivating cross-domain work notes that metric methods succeed when novel classes are sampled from the same domain as meta-training, as in miniImageNet train/test splits, but often generalize poorly when novel categories come from a different domain such as CUB or Cars after training on miniImageNet. Consequently, methods evaluated only on same-domain episodes provide evidence for unseen-class transfer within an approximately shared visual domain, not evidence for broad domain transfer. This distinction is essential when comparing K-tuplet, ICNN, ADM, SRL, and multi-stage models because their cross-domain protocols and target datasets are not identical. [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:0:da237bb5f22f:claim:39aa02f3d33c] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:abstract:claim:823c76c237f3]

Large-scale transfer learning is a competing route to few-shot adaptation rather than a metric-learning mechanism. In the VTAB plus Meta-Dataset cross-family study, BiT-L is established as strong on the unified protocol, and large-scale transfer methods outperform competing approaches on average on Meta-Dataset even when trained only on ImageNet; the same study finds that meta-learning approaches trained and validated on Meta-Dataset struggle to compete on VTAB. These findings are relevant context for why metric methods must be compared against representation scale, but they do not show that metric learning is obsolete. BiT-L also does not dominate every Meta-Dataset source, with Omniglot and QuickDraw identified as sources where its scale advantage does not make it better than competing approaches. [E:arxiv:2104.02638:abstract:claim:727abcd8e3b1] [E:arxiv:2104.02638:abstract:claim:1ad165a11aa4] [E:arxiv:2104.02638:section:abstract:2:baccf9bc87dd:claim:76401b33d078] [E:arxiv:2104.02638:section:abstract:1:f6c575ccd9aa:claim:6dc5641724f0] [E:arxiv:2104.02638:section:abstract:2:baccf9bc87dd:claim:ecf4ad2d5e3a]

Across these methods, the strongest mechanistic comparison is therefore complementary rather than a single winner. Instance matching minimizes assumptions but depends directly on support examples; prototypes stabilize class summaries as points; distribution and subspace models encode uncertainty or variation; learned, asymmetric, region-based, and task-conditioned comparators increase relational flexibility; K-tuplet, Proto-Triplet, and ICNN primarily shape embedding geometry; and multi-stage encoders enrich the features entering the metric. Applicability should be judged jointly with data domain, shot count, backbone, training scale, and evaluation protocol, rather than inferring universal superiority from one benchmark result. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:abstract:claim:92863cf84848] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_few_shot_deep_metric_learning_methods:0:c53378070ee7:claim:65f78a914028] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:41e8ea8f67cc] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:abstract:1:672489eb0fa9:claim:b75d4ecca446] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:421a9600bb91]

## Comparative Evidence Analysis

Experimental comparisons should first be read by benchmark and episode protocol. The standard image setting is 5-way 1-shot or 5-shot episodic classification, but papers vary in backbone, training split, data augmentation, pre-training, query count, episode sampling, and whether test classes come from the same dataset or a different domain. The cross-family VTAB+MD study makes this caution explicit: transfer-learning and meta-learning advances have often used different evaluation norms, so results produced under different protocols are not directly rankable. Accordingly, the comparisons below group evidence by what was actually matched rather than merging all reported accuracies into one leaderboard. [E:arxiv:2104.02638:abstract:claim:727abcd8e3b1] [E:arxiv:2104.02638:section:abstract:1:f6c575ccd9aa:claim:6dc5641724f0] [E:arxiv:2104.02638:section:abstract:2:baccf9bc87dd:claim:ecf4ad2d5e3a]

Within same-domain miniImageNet-style evaluation, the main comparison axis is which metric-learning stage is changed. Matching Networks provide the instance-comparison endpoint with an end-to-end k-nearest-neighbor-like rule; Prototypical Networks summarize support examples into class prototypes; and Relation Networks replace fixed cosine or Euclidean comparison with a learned nonlinear relation score. The K-tuplet paper characterizes these as metric baselines and reports that its embedding-focused deep K-tuplet method outperforms other metric-based approaches on miniImageNet. That comparison supports improved feature geometry under the paper's episodic setup, but it does not by itself establish superiority over later prototype, comparator, or transfer methods unless those methods use the same backbone and training budget. [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:3:11bb8b6bf73e:claim:b3038684f21d] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:1:f6a11fe47f73:claim:852780aa640e] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:abstract:claim:823c76c237f3]

The K-tuplet result is especially informative because it reports both in-domain and cross-dataset tests from a model trained on miniImageNet. In-domain testing uses held-out miniImageNet classes, while cross-domain testing transfers the trained model to Caltech-101, CUB-200, Stanford Dogs, and Stanford Cars. The authors state that their method outperforms prior methods in this cross-dataset protocol, which is evidence that jointly comparing an anchor with multiple negatives can improve transferable embeddings. However, the appropriate comparison is against methods evaluated in that same train-on-miniImageNet, test-on-other-datasets protocol; it should not be compared numerically with models trained on the target dataset or with large-scale transfer models trained on broader upstream data. [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:3:11bb8b6bf73e:claim:b3038684f21d] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:2:4c9f8b613811:claim:5c1b3aa35115] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:abstract:claim:823c76c237f3]

Loss-level embedding methods provide a second same-domain versus cross-domain evidence pattern. Proto-Triplet Loss and ICNN Loss modify training geometry by enforcing more suitable intra-class and inter-class relationships in episodic embedding space; the paper reports about a 2% accuracy margin over compared metric-based methods on miniImageNet and competitive generalization to Caltech, CUB, Dogs, and Cars. These results are directly about the contribution of the loss functions under the authors' extensive setup. They are not evidence that loss shaping dominates richer class representations or learned comparators in general, because the cited abstract does not provide matched numerical tables for every alternative architecture and training recipe. [E:arxiv:2305.09062:abstract:claim:24974efbef21] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:abstract:claim:1b369d5d7d5f]

Class-representation and comparator innovations are supported on different benchmark slices. The target-conditioned classifier paper reports state-of-the-art performance on the Caltech-UCSD Birds fine-grained classification task, using target-conditioned class representations and a network that performs comparisons rather than relying on a static metric. This is a strong task-specific result for fine-grained recognition, where query-relevant region or appearance differences can matter. It is not directly comparable to a miniImageNet average or to a tieredImageNet result, because CUB changes the class structure toward visually similar bird species and the paper's architecture and training setting are specific to that evaluation. [E:arxiv:1802.04376:section:abstract:4:8531e2861789:claim:b08bca94e51c] [E:arxiv:1802.04376:abstract:claim:dfbfdad30c36]

ADM supplies a matched 5-way 1-shot comparison on two standard few-shot datasets, but the available source gives relative gains rather than a full table of absolute accuracies. On miniImageNet and tieredImageNet, the asymmetric distribution-measure network reports gains of 3.02% and 1.56%, respectively, over the state-of-the-art method on the 5-way 1-shot task. These values are percentage-point accuracy gains if reported on the papers' accuracy scale, and they support the authors' claim that asymmetric local-and-global distributional comparison helps the 1-shot setting. They should not be converted into a ranking over 5-shot methods or over methods absent from that state-of-the-art comparison, and the source does not establish identical gains on other domains. [E:arxiv:2002.00153:abstract:claim:68151909197b]

Subspace representation learning is evaluated on MiniImageNet, TieredImageNet, and CUB. The framework represents images with local-CNN subspaces, uses weighted subspace distance, and aggregates K-shot support information with prototypical or discriminative template subspaces. The paper reports competitive or superior performance relative to prior state-of-the-art methods across those public benchmarks. This supports the geometric claim that preserving spatial structure and feature diversity can be useful, but the phrase competitive/superior is not a single numerical win across every setting; 1-shot, 5-shot, dataset, and template-subspace choices must remain attached to the paper's table-level results rather than being summarized as a universal ranking. [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:8a4c1729167e] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:02380d44985c]

The review-level subspace evidence adds a qualitative robustness comparison rather than a cross-benchmark score. Deep Subspace Network constructs class-specific low-dimensional subspaces from support samples by singular value decomposition and classifies a query by the nearest subspace, using the distance between the query and its projection. The review states that this approach is more robust to noise and outliers than Prototypical Networks. That comparison is specifically about sensitivity to noisy or outlying support points under the subspace-versus-prototype mechanisms; it does not imply higher accuracy on every dataset or lower computational cost, because subspace construction and projection introduce their own operations and assumptions. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:421a9600bb91]

RCN's experiments are organized around both effectiveness and interpretability on four benchmark datasets. The method learns corresponding regions between query and support images, visualizes intermediate comparisons with Region Activation Mapping, and extends interpretation from individual tasks toward category-level prototypical parts. The paper states that experiments clearly show effectiveness over existing baselines and demonstrates the visualization and prototype-finding components. Thus RCN should be evaluated on two separate dimensions: classification performance against matched baselines and explanation behavior. A visualization result does not prove that the attended regions causally determine the class, and the abstract-level source does not provide enough numerical detail to rank RCN against all later metric methods. [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:introduction:3:fb29f917e0e2:claim:899fa0448e5a] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:introduction:3:fb29f917e0e2:claim:9f8299b19a8c] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:abstract:0:94ff5952b4c1:claim:75c753f3205c]

Multi-stage embedding evidence covers both standard and cross-domain tests but remains architecture-specific. MSENet is evaluated on MiniImageNet and FC100 in 5-way 1-shot and 5-way 5-shot scenarios and on cross-domain tasks across eight benchmark datasets; it combines multi-output features, self-attention at multiple stages, and learnable stage weights. The reported high accuracy supports using shallow and deep feature spaces together, but the cited source does not supply the matched per-dataset numbers needed here to compare it numerically with K-tuplet, ADM, SRL, or RCN. Its results are therefore evidence for the multi-stage design within that implementation, not a benchmark-independent ranking. [E:arxiv:2409.07989:abstract:claim:baa36cba9b0a]

Hybrid and task-adaptive metric learning addresses a setting that ordinary fixed-metric comparisons may not cover. Meta-Metric-Learner is tested both in the standard k-shot N-way setting and in a realistic setting with flexible class counts, in single-source and multi-source forms, and the authors report superior performance across those settings. The relevant comparison is therefore not only accuracy on a fixed 5-way episode, but also ability to handle variable-way tasks and multiple task sources. A fixed 5-way score from another paper cannot establish superiority or inferiority on flexible-class or multi-source evaluation, because the task distribution and adaptation target differ. [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:3b48d1371831] [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:f090d17c92ce] [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:c7b491e4de94]

Cross-family results provide an outer boundary for interpreting metric-learning gains. In the unified VTAB+MD study, BiT-L is established as strong on the combined protocol; large-scale transfer methods outperform competing approaches on average on Meta-Dataset even when trained only on ImageNet, while meta-learning approaches trained and validated on Meta-Dataset struggle to compete on VTAB. The same study notes that scale does not help uniformly across Meta-Dataset sources and identifies Omniglot and QuickDraw as cases where BiT-L does no better than competing approaches despite larger data and architecture size. These findings compare families under a deliberately unified protocol, but they should not be used to dismiss metric methods evaluated only on miniImageNet, nor to infer that metric-learning design choices are irrelevant once scale changes. [E:arxiv:2104.02638:abstract:claim:727abcd8e3b1] [E:arxiv:2104.02638:abstract:claim:1ad165a11aa4] [E:arxiv:2104.02638:section:abstract:2:baccf9bc87dd:claim:76401b33d078] [E:arxiv:2104.02638:section:abstract:2:baccf9bc87dd:claim:ecf4ad2d5e3a]

Domain-specific benchmarks further limit generalization claims. The FewSAR study for synthetic-aperture-radar target images implements 15 classic methods in three categories, uses unified protocols, and analyzes both quantitative results and runtime; it reports that metric-learning methods achieve the best accuracy, while meta-learning and fine-tuning methods perform poorly, with the authors attributing this primarily to bias in existing datasets. This is evidence for metric learning on FewSAR under that benchmark's imagery and labels, not evidence that the same ranking holds for natural-image datasets such as miniImageNet or CUB. Runtime measured in that SAR setting also cannot be generalized to other backbones or image resolutions. [E:arxiv:2306.09592:abstract:claim:a84f557f7113]

Taken together, the experimental evidence supports localized comparisons rather than one universal winner. Embedding-loss methods such as K-tuplet, Proto-Triplet, and ICNN show strong miniImageNet and cross-dataset transfer evidence; ADM gives explicit 1-shot gains on miniImageNet and tieredImageNet; SRL and DSN test subspace geometry on MiniImageNet, TieredImageNet, CUB, and noise-robustness terms; target-conditioned comparison is especially tied to CUB fine-grained classification; RCN adds region-level interpretability; MSENet tests multi-stage features on MiniImageNet, FC100, and eight cross-domain tasks; and Meta-Metric-Learner addresses flexible and multi-source tasks. Because datasets, backbones, training sources, shot counts, target domains, and adaptation rules differ across these studies, the defensible conclusion is a comparison of evidence coverage and mechanism, not an invented overall ranking. ## Limitations and Open Problems

The first open problem is that the three metric-learning stages are not equally reliable when support data are extremely scarce. Early instance-to-instance comparison avoids constructing a class model, but a single support image gives little protection against atypical pose, background, or appearance. Point prototypes reduce dependence on one example by averaging support embeddings, yet a single vector can suppress within-class variation and remains sensitive to outliers; the review literature therefore motivates distributional or subspace representations as ways to model uncertainty, spatial structure, and diversity. These richer models do not remove the estimation problem: with only one or a few support examples, a distribution, subspace, or learned comparator may itself be poorly constrained. The practical implication is that representation complexity should be interpreted relative to shot count and support quality rather than assumed to scale monotonically with accuracy. [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_learning_class_representations:0:45daa993ea6a:claim:41e8ea8f67cc] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:section:2_2_3_distribution_or_subspace_based_representations:0:f1e8e9a53553:claim:421a9600bb91] [E:arxiv:2002.00153:abstract:claim:68151909197b] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:8a4c1729167e]

A second problem is the gap between same-domain novel-class evaluation and cross-domain deployment. Standard miniImageNet-style episodes test whether features transfer to unseen classes drawn from a broadly similar visual domain, whereas training on miniImageNet and testing on CUB, Cars, Dogs, Caltech-101, or other datasets changes the visual distribution as well as the labels. The cross-domain metric-learning study explicitly notes that existing metric approaches often do not generalize well to categories from different domains. K-tuplet and later embedding-loss methods report cross-dataset evidence, but those results support robustness under their particular train-source and target-domain protocols; they do not imply that a metric learned on one source will remain calibrated on every domain. [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:0:da237bb5f22f:claim:39aa02f3d33c] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:2:4c9f8b613811:claim:5c1b3aa35115] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:abstract:claim:823c76c237f3] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:abstract:claim:24974efbef21] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:abstract:claim:1b369d5d7d5f]

Task heterogeneity exposes a related limitation of a single task-invariant metric. Meta-Metric-Learner is motivated by the observation that a common metric can accommodate different class counts but may fail when tasks come from domains that require different metrics, while optimization-based meta-learning can specify task models but has traditionally imposed more homogeneous task structure. The adaptive-metric evidence from diverse natural-language tasks independently identifies the same conceptual issue: one metric may be insufficient when task variation is large. For image classification, this means that fixed Euclidean, cosine, or even globally learned relation functions are best justified when meta-training and test episodes share enough structure; flexible-way, multi-source, or heterogeneous-domain settings may require task-specific metric adaptation. [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:3b48d1371831] [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:f090d17c92ce] [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:c7b491e4de94] [E:arxiv:1805.07513:abstract:claim:8090ccd62bec]

Learned comparators create a flexibility-versus-reliability trade-off. Relation Networks and target-conditioned comparison networks can express nonlinear, query-dependent relations that fixed distances cannot, and target-conditioned class representations can emphasize features relevant to a particular comparison. However, that flexibility is learned from episodic data and therefore depends on the coverage and quality of meta-training episodes. It also does not separately guarantee that the support-class summary is accurate or that the learned relation is semantically stable. Consequently, a learned comparator should not be treated as a universal correction for weak embeddings, noisy support sets, or domain shift. [E:arxiv:1711.06025:abstract:claim:1a5f717da016] [E:arxiv:1802.04376:section:abstract:4:8531e2861789:claim:b08bca94e51c] [E:arxiv:1802.04376:abstract:claim:dfbfdad30c36] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:1:f6a11fe47f73:claim:852780aa640e]

Embedding-geometry losses address an important bottleneck but leave other bottlenecks unresolved. K-tuplet learning compares an anchor with multiple negatives and uses semi-hard mining to improve convergence stability and discriminative geometry; Proto-Triplet and ICNN losses similarly shape intra-class and inter-class distances. These mechanisms can improve the latent space entering a nearest-neighbor, prototype, or nonlinear classifier, but they do not by themselves define a richer class distribution, a task-dependent comparator, or a domain-adaptation procedure. A model can therefore have well-separated base-class geometry and still fail when novel support examples are outliers, when classes are fine-grained, or when the target domain differs strongly from meta-training. [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:2:4c9f8b613811:claim:6ec2ea7e56e2] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:section:abstract:2:4c9f8b613811:claim:5c1b3aa35115] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:abstract:claim:24974efbef21] [E:arxiv:2305.09062:abstract:claim:1b369d5d7d5f] [E:arxiv:1907.03123:abstract:claim:823c76c237f3]

Local, region-based, and multi-stage representations improve information use but add design and validation burdens. RCN learns corresponding regions and provides Region Activation Mapping and category-level prototypical parts, while MSENet combines features from multiple network stages, self-attention, and learnable stage weights. These designs can recover shallow or spatially localized information that a single global vector misses. The limitation is that visualizations are not causal proof that the highlighted regions are the correct basis for classification, and multi-stage attention plus learned weighting introduces extra parameters and implementation choices. Their benefits therefore need matched ablation and baseline comparisons rather than being inferred solely from qualitative maps or aggregate accuracy. [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:abstract:0:94ff5952b4c1:claim:75c753f3205c] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:introduction:3:fb29f917e0e2:claim:899fa0448e5a] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:introduction:3:fb29f917e0e2:claim:9f8299b19a8c] [E:arxiv:2409.07989:abstract:claim:baa36cba9b0a]

Interpretability remains a distinct and incompletely solved objective. RCN's region correspondences and activation maps make some intermediate metric computations inspectable, and its prototype-part extraction extends explanation from a task toward category-level evidence. Nevertheless, the cited method demonstrates visualization and decision-support explanations, not a general guarantee that the attended regions are causally sufficient, stable across episodes, or aligned with human category definitions. This distinction matters in few-shot classification because a model may produce plausible local explanations while relying on background, dataset bias, or incidental co-occurrence. [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:abstract:0:94ff5952b4c1:claim:75c753f3205c] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:introduction:3:fb29f917e0e2:claim:899fa0448e5a] [E:arxiv:2009.03558:section:introduction:3:fb29f917e0e2:claim:9f8299b19a8c]

Evaluation fragmentation is a central obstacle to scientific comparison. The VTAB+MD study argues that transfer-learning and meta-learning communities have used divergent evaluation norms, making direct or thorough comparison difficult, and it deliberately combines Meta-Dataset and VTAB to test whether methods transfer across benchmarks. Within metric learning, the problem is also visible at smaller scale: papers use different backbones, pre-training sources, data augmentations, episode samplers, target datasets, and same-domain versus cross-domain splits. Relative gains such as ADM's 3.02% on miniImageNet and 1.56% on tieredImageNet for 5-way 1-shot, or statements of competitive and superior performance for subspace methods, are meaningful only with the baseline set and protocol used by each paper. [E:arxiv:2104.02638:abstract:claim:727abcd8e3b1] [E:arxiv:2104.02638:section:abstract:1:f6c575ccd9aa:claim:6dc5641724f0] [E:arxiv:2104.02638:section:abstract:2:baccf9bc87dd:claim:ecf4ad2d5e3a] [E:arxiv:2002.00153:abstract:claim:68151909197b] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:8a4c1729167e] [E:arxiv:2105.00379:abstract:claim:02380d44985c]

Scale and representation learning can alter the interpretation of episodic metric innovations. The cross-family study finds that large-scale transfer methods, particularly BiT, perform strongly on average on Meta-Dataset under the unified VTAB+MD protocol, while meta-learning methods trained and validated on Meta-Dataset have difficulty competing on VTAB. At the same time, scale is not uniformly decisive: Omniglot and QuickDraw are identified as Meta-Dataset sources where BiT-L does no better than competing approaches despite larger data and architecture size. Thus, comparisons between metric-learning methods and large transfer baselines must control upstream data, architecture size, resolution, normalization, and adaptation rules; otherwise an apparent algorithmic gain may reflect scale rather than the metric. [E:arxiv:2104.02638:abstract:claim:727abcd8e3b1] [E:arxiv:2104.02638:abstract:claim:1ad165a11aa4] [E:arxiv:2104.02638:section:abstract:2:baccf9bc87dd:claim:76401b33d078] [E:arxiv:2104.02638:section:abstract:2:baccf9bc87dd:claim:ecf4ad2d5e3a]

Finally, evidence from specialized domains should not be over-generalized. The FewSAR benchmark reports that metric-learning methods achieve the best accuracy under its unified SAR target-image protocols, while meta-learning and fine-tuning methods perform poorly, an outcome the authors attribute partly to bias in existing datasets. That result supports metric learning for the studied SAR setting, but SAR imagery, class structure, and dataset bias differ materially from natural-image benchmarks. Together with the protocol and domain-shift issues above, the open problem is not merely to improve average 5-way accuracy, but to establish which embedding, class-representation, and comparison choices remain useful across matched shot counts, domains, model scales, task structures, and explanation requirements. [E:arxiv:2306.09592:abstract:claim:a84f557f7113] [E:arxiv:2001.08735:section:1_introduction:0:da237bb5f22f:claim:39aa02f3d33c] [E:arxiv:2104.02638:section:abstract:1:f6c575ccd9aa:claim:6dc5641724f0] [E:arxiv:1904.03014:abstract:claim:3b48d1371831] [E:arxiv:2105.08149:abstract:claim:92863cf84848]

## Conclusion

Metric-learning methods should be compared by the bottleneck they address, not by one accuracy ordering. Instance matching makes the weakest class-model assumption but depends directly on support quality; prototypes stabilize classes as points but can hide variation and remain sensitive to outliers; distributional and subspace models represent uncertainty, spatial structure, and diversity but may be underconstrained in 1-shot tasks. Fixed metrics are simpler and more interpretable, whereas learned, asymmetric, query-conditioned, region-based, or task-adaptive comparators express more context-dependent relations but require suitable episodic coverage and cannot repair weak embeddings or noisy support sets by themselves. Embedding losses and multi-stage encoders improve inputs to the decision rule without resolving class-summary or domain-shift choices. The central trade-off is representational richness against estimability, complexity, and transfer breadth. Evidence must stay attached to same-domain novel classes, cross-dataset targets after miniImageNet training, CUB fine-grained categories, flexible-way or multi-source tasks, large-scale transfer protocols, or SAR data. For example, ADM's gains are specific to 5-way 1-shot miniImageNet and tieredImageNet, and BiT-L's strong average Meta-Dataset result does not extend uniformly to Omniglot and QuickDraw. Method choice should therefore match shot count, support quality, domain heterogeneity, task structure, scale, and interpretability needs. claim_records.text: The proposed deep K-tuplet network extends the classical triplet network from deep metric learning for few-shot learning, utilizing the relationship among input samples to learn a general representation via episode-training.

The trained network can extract discriminative features for unseen novel categories and can be seamlessly incorporated with a non-linear distance metric function to facilitate few-shot classification.
The method's result on the miniImageNet benchmark outperforms other metric-based few-shot classification methods.
When evaluated on Caltech-101, CUB-200, Stanford Dogs and Cars using the model trained with miniImageNet, the method significantly outperforms prior methods.

The deep K-tuplet Network generalizes the triplet network to allow joint comparison with K negative samples in each mini-batch, making feature embedding learning more faithful to few-shot classification with improved feature generalization.
The semi-hard mining sampling technique is presented as an effective sampling strategy to sample informative hard triplets, speeding up convergence and stabilizing training procedure.
The method achieves competitive performance over other meta-based methods on the miniImageNet benchmark.

A new experimental setting is established for evaluating cross-domain generalization ability of few-shot classification algorithms, with results on CUB-200, Stanford Dogs, Stanford Cars and Caltech-101 excelling other methods.

The method performs target tasks based entirely on feed-forward without requiring further parameter updates, unlike meta-learning methods that need fine-tuning or parameter updates for new unseen tasks.
The relation network learns a nonlinear distance metric via a shallow neural network instead of using fixed linear distance metrics such as Cosine and Euclidean.

claim_records.text: Two loss functions are proposed for few-shot image classification: Proto-Triplet Loss, based on original triplet loss modified for few-shot scenarios, and ICNN loss, based on inter and intra class nearest neighbors score.
The proposed loss functions show a significant improvement in accuracy in the miniImageNet benchmark compared to other metric-based few-shot learning methods by a margin of 2%.
The proposed methods demonstrate competitive generalization capabilities to other domains including Caltech, CUB, Dogs and Cars datasets compared with the state of the art.
Using proto-triplet loss, the method obtains 61.32% accuracy in the 5-way 1-shot setting and 79.93% accuracy in the 5-way 5-shot setting on the Mini-Imagenet dataset.
Using ICNN Loss, the method obtains 60.79% accuracy in the 5-way 1-shot setting and 80.41% accuracy in the 5-way 5-shot setting on the Mini-Imagenet dataset.

The ICNN Loss evaluates the quality of features obtained based on inter/intra class distance, variance and class ratio from nearest neighbors, assigning each data point an Inter and Intra Class Nearest Neighbors score.
The Proto-Triplet Loss takes a query point as anchor, the prototype from the same class as positive point and the nearest prototype of different class as the negative point.
Both proposed loss functions aim to increase the inter-class distance and decrease the intra-class distance between samples of different classes.
The proposed methods are further tested on CUB, Caltech, Stanford Dogs and Stanford Cars datasets to assess generalization capabilities, obtaining satisfactory results.

claim_records.text: The introduced Metric-Agnostic Conditional network (MACO) architecture achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Caltech-UCSD birds fine-grained classification task.
The MACO architecture deviates from traditional metric-learning approaches by training a network to perform comparisons between classes rather than relying on a static metric comparison.
The MACO architecture is not a true metric-learning approach, as its output is a softmax probability distribution rather than a true distance or similarity metric.
The MACO network achieves its best performance only when it is allowed to condition each class representation based on the target (query) image.
The MACO network consists of four distinct stages trained fully end-to-end: Feature Stage, Relational Stage, Conditioning Stage, and Classifier.

The Feature Stage of MACO uses a convolutional architecture with four convolutional blocks, each containing a 2D convolutional layer with 3×3 kernel and 32 filters, followed by batch normalization, ELU activation, and 2×2 max pooling, with a final linear layer producing an 800-dimensional vector.

The Relational Stage of MACO uses relational networks to compare images within a class in a pairwise fashion, producing a single vector to represent the class, with parameters shared across all classes.
The Conditioning Stage of MACO uses the query image to augment the representation for each class.
The Classifier stage of MACO combines information across class vectors and makes a final softmax classification based on the query image.
Initial experiments with dropout as a regularizer in the MACO feature stage showed poor convergence during training and were therefore excluded.
Initial experiments indicate the MACO model also works well with a larger, pre-trained ResNet architecture.
Relational networks in the MACO Relational Stage compare images within a class pairwise, with the number of comparisons scaling quadratically with the number of images n in the class.

claim_records.text: The proposed Meta-Metric-Learner hybrid meta-learning model combines optimization-based and metric-based meta-learning approaches, consisting of a task-specific metric-based learner as a base model and a meta-learner that learns and specifies the base model.
The Meta-Metric-Learner model is able to handle flexible numbers of classes as well as generate more generalized metrics for classification across tasks.

Experiments show that the Meta-Metric-Learner approach obtains superior performance in both the standard k-shot N-way few-shot learning setting and a new realistic few-shot setting with flexible class numbers in both single-source and multi-source forms.

Existing optimization-based few-shot learning approaches require task-specific classifiers to be homogeneous-structured to ease parameter prediction, so they can only handle few-shot learning problems where tasks share a uniform number of classes.
Existing metric-based few-shot learning approaches learn one task-invariant metric for all tasks, requiring tasks to come from a similar domain such that a uniform metric works across tasks.
The meta learner in Meta-Metric-Learner operates across tasks using an optimization-based meta-model to discover good parameters and gradient descent in task-specific base learners.
The base learner in Meta-Metric-Learner exploits a metric-based model and parameterizes task metrics using weight prediction from the optimization-based meta-learner.
The Meta-Metric-Learner model is able to handle unbalanced classes in meta-train and meta-test sets because it uses metric-based learners.
The Meta-Metric-Learner generates task-specific metrics leveraging weight prediction of the meta-learner given task instances, so that metrics adapt better to different tasks.
The learned task-invariant metric of existing metric-based approaches may not generalize well if tasks diverge.
In real-world few-shot learning applications where tasks come from different domains or data sources, it is unlikely that a uniform metric is suitable for all tasks.

Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) explicitly trains the initial parameters of a CNN model such that a small number of gradient update steps with a small amount of training data from a new task will produce good generalization performance on that task.
Meta-SGD extends MAML by learning to learn not just the learner initialization, but also the learner update direction and learning rate.
TAML presents an entropy-based approach to avoid a biased meta-learner and improve its generalizability to new tasks.

claim_records.text: A single metric is insufficient to capture complex task variations in the natural language domain for diverse few-shot learning tasks.
The proposed adaptive metric learning approach automatically determines the best weighted combination from a set of metrics obtained from meta-training tasks for a newly seen few-shot task.

Extensive quantitative evaluations on real-world sentiment analysis and dialog intent classification datasets show the proposed method performs favorably against state-of-the-art few-shot learning algorithms in terms of predictive accuracy.

The proposed task-clustering framework for diverse few-shot learning starts with a novel task clustering algorithm based on matrix completion, followed by a few-shot learning method based on task clustering.

fact_fields.method: Task-clustering framework with matrix completion-based task clustering

claim_records.text: Directly using transfer performance for task clustering requires conducting source-target transfer learning O(n^2) times, where n is the number of meta-training tasks.
When the number of meta-training tasks n exceeds 1000, evaluating the full transfer performance matrix involves over 1M entries, which is unacceptable.
The proposed matrix completion-based task clustering algorithm randomly samples task pairs to evaluate S_ij and S_ji scores to address the large number of entries in the transfer performance matrix.
The proposed matrix completion-based task clustering algorithm keeps only task pairs (i, j) with consistent S_ij and S_ji scores to address unreliable entries and asymmetry issues.

Previous few-shot learning works mainly considered image domains such as Omniglot and ImageNet, where tasks are sampled from a single data collection and thus related, employing a common meta-model for all few-shot tasks.
In enterprise AI cloud service scenarios, client-submitted text classification tasks are significantly diverse, making a common metric insufficient to handle all tasks.

Few-shot learning aims to learn classifiers from few examples per class via meta-models learned from a large number of meta-training tasks for rapid adaptation to target tasks with few training examples.

claim_records.text: Deep metric learning methods classify unseen samples according to their distances to few seen samples in an embedding space learned by deep neural networks, avoiding overfitting to few training images in few-shot image classification.

The review categorizes deep metric learning methods for few-shot image classification from 2018 to 2022 into three groups according to three stages of metric learning: learning feature embeddings, learning class representations, and learning distance measures.

In few-shot classification, the metric is learned on the base dataset, and query images of novel classes are classified by computing distances to novel support images with respect to the learned measure, followed by a distance-based classifier such as k-nearest neighbors.

fact_fields.method: Supervised metric learning for few-shot classification

claim_records.text: Early few-shot metric learning methods such as Siamese Network and Matching Network classify a query sample by measuring and comparing its distance to support samples, but support samples are scarce and have limited capacity in representing the novel class.
Class prototypes serve as reference vectors for each class, constructed by simple or weighted average of feature embeddings or learned end-to-end to improve representation ability.

Zhang et al. proposed a variational Bayesian framework for few-shot learning that uses Kullback-Leibler divergence to measure sample distance and computes query class assignment confidence by estimating each class distribution via a neural network.

fact_fields.method: Variational Bayesian framework for few-shot learning

claim_records.text: Simon et al. proposed Deep Subspace Network (DSN) to represent each class using a low-dimensional subspace constructed from support samples via singular value decomposition, classifying queries by nearest subspace classifier based on shortest Euclidean distance between query and its projection onto the class-specific subspace.
Deep Subspace Network (DSN) is more robust to noises and outliers than Prototypical Network.

claim_records.text: The Uncertainty-Aware Few-Shot (UAFS) framework models uncertainty of query-prototype similarity and performs uncertainty-aware optimization for image classification.

Rather than using a scalar, the similarity between a query feature zi and a prototype feature cj is modeled by a distribution (probabilistic similarity) based on graph-based similarity uncertainty estimation.

For a query sample xi and N prototypes in the support set, each query-prototype pair is treated as a node and a graph-based model is employed to jointly infer the similarity uncertainty σi,j for each query-prototype pair.
The network is optimized with similarity-based classification losses which exploit the estimated uncertainty.
Few-shot image classification aims to classify query samples of new categories given only a few labeled support samples of these categories as examples.

In few-shot image classification, the feature embeddings of support samples of a category are averaged to form the prototype of that category, and the set of prototypes acts as a similarity-based classifier to identify the category of a query sample by finding the nearest prototype over the support set in the embedding space.

fact_fields.method: prototype averaging of support sample feature embeddings

claim_records.text: During training, for a query sample, the logit vector (classification probability) is obtained by feeding the similarities between the query sample and the prototypes to a SoftMax function.

fact_fields.method: SoftMax function applied to query-prototype similarities

claim_records.text: The reliability of the estimated similarity is vital to the classification performance in few-shot image classification.
Aleatoric uncertainty identifies the confidence level of the network on its output for a sample, capturing the noise inherent in the observations.
For few-shot image classification, the network has different uncertainties on the calculated similarities of different query-prototype pairs.
An observed similarity of a query-prototype pair, being a one time sampling, suffers from observation noise, where higher uncertainty corresponds to less reliable estimated similarity.
For each few-shot task during optimization, the number of experienced query-prototype pairs is limited, and the side effect of observation noises due to high uncertainty limits the optimization.

For each query-prototype pair, the observed feature similarity between the query and the prototype is converted from a deterministic scalar to a distribution, with the variance of this distribution characterizing the uncertainty of the observed similarity.

fact_fields.method: conversion of observed feature similarity from scalar to distribution

claim_records.text: The similarity-based classification losses are calculated based on the converted probabilistic similarity representations.

claim_records.text: Existing metric-based few-shot classification algorithms often fail to generalize to unseen domains due to large discrepancy of feature distribution across domains.

The core idea of the proposed method is to use feature-wise transformation layers for augmenting image features using affine transforms to simulate various feature distributions under different domains in the training stage.

fact_fields.method: feature-wise transformation layers with affine transforms

claim_records.text: A learning-to-learn approach is applied to search for the hyper-parameters of the feature-wise transformation layers to capture variations of feature distributions under different domains.
Extensive experiments and ablation studies are conducted under the domain generalization setting using five few-shot classification datasets: mini-ImageNet, CUB, Cars, Places, and Plantae.
The proposed feature-wise transformation layer is applicable to various metric-based models and provides consistent improvements on few-shot classification performance under domain shift.
Metric-based few-shot classification methods consist of a feature encoder and a metric function, making predictions based on the similarity between query images and support examples.
The feature encoder first extracts image features, and the metric function takes features of both labeled and unlabeled images as input to predict the category of query images.
Existing metric-based approaches do not generalize well to categories from different domains.
The distributions of image features extracted from tasks in unseen domains are significantly different from those in seen domains.
Unsupervised domain adaptation approaches assume that numerous unlabeled images are available in the target domain during training.
Domain generalization methods learn classifiers that generalize well to multiple unseen domains without requiring access to data from those domains.
During training, the metric function may overfit to feature distributions encoded only from seen domains and thus fail to generalize to unseen domains.

Feature-wise transformation layers integrated into the feature encoder modulate feature activations with affine transformations to simulate various distributions of image features during training, improving the generalization ability of the metric function in the testing phase.

fact_fields.method: feature-wise transformation layers integrated into feature encoder

claim_records.text: The hyper-parameters of feature-wise transformation layers may require meticulous hand-tuning due to the difficulty to model complex variation of image feature distributions across various domains.
A learning-to-learn algorithm is developed to optimize the proposed feature-wise transformation layers so that the model can work well on unseen domains after training using seen domains.
The proposed feature-wise transformation layers are method-agnostic and can be applied to various metric-based few-shot classification approaches for improving their generalization to unseen domains.

claim_records.text: The Relation Network (RN) is trained end-to-end from scratch for few-shot learning.
During meta-learning, RN learns a deep distance metric to compare images within episodes designed to simulate the few-shot setting.
Once trained, RN classifies images of new classes by computing relation scores between query images and few examples of each new class without further network updates.
The RN framework is easily extended to zero-shot learning in addition to few-shot learning.
Extensive experiments on five benchmarks demonstrate the RN approach provides a unified and effective method for both few-shot and zero-shot learning tasks.
RN provides improved performance on few-shot learning compared to prior approaches.

claim_records.text: Existing CLIP-based few-shot classification approaches such as CoOp and Tip-Adapter only focus on high-level visual features fully aligned with textual features representing the summary of an image.
Local representations (LRs) at low-level are more consistent between seen and unseen samples than high-level representations for few-shot classification.
The proposed MF-Adapter combines complementary strengths of low-level local representations and high-level semantic representations for few-shot classification.
The Meta-Feature Unit (MF-Unit) is a simple yet effective local similarity metric that measures category-consistent local context in an inductive manner.
MF-Adapter is trained to map image features to MF-Unit to generalize intra-class knowledge between unseen images and the support set.
Extensive experiments show MF-Adapter outperforms state-of-the-art CLIP downstream few-shot classification methods, with stronger performance on challenging visual classification tasks.

claim_records.text: Prototypical networks are proposed for few-shot classification, where a classifier must generalize to new classes not seen in the training set given only a small number of examples of each new class.
Prototypical networks learn a metric space in which classification can be performed by computing distances to prototype representations of each class.
Compared to recent approaches for few-shot learning, prototypical networks reflect a simpler inductive bias that is beneficial in the limited-data regime and achieve excellent results.
An analysis shows that some simple design decisions can yield substantial improvements over recent approaches involving complicated architectural choices and meta-learning.

claim_records.text: The subspace representation learning (SRL) framework represents an image by exploiting a subspace in local CNN feature space, and measures similarity between two images according to a weighted subspace distance (WSD).

When K images are available for each class, the SRL framework develops two types of template subspaces to aggregate K-shot information: the prototypical subspace (PS) and the discriminative subspace (DS).
The SRL framework extends metric learning based techniques from vector to subspace representation.
Using subspace representation can effectively preserve the spatial structure and diversity within an image, in contrast to most previous works that adopted global vector representation.

Experiments on three public benchmark datasets (MiniImageNet, TieredImageNet, and Caltech-UCSD Birds-200-2011 (CUB)) illustrate competitive/superior performance of the SRL method compared to the previous state-of-the-art.

claim_records.text: The core idea of metric-based few-shot image classification is to directly measure the relations between query images and support classes to learn transferable feature embeddings.
Previous work mainly focusing on image-level feature representations cannot effectively estimate a class's distribution due to the scarcity of samples.
Some recent work shows that local descriptor based representations can achieve richer representations than image-level based representations.
Existing local descriptor based works are still based on a less effective instance-level metric, especially a symmetric metric, to measure the relations between query images and support classes.
Given the natural asymmetric relation between a query image and a support class, an asymmetric measure is more suitable for metric-based few-shot learning.
The Asymmetric Distribution Measure (ADM) network for few-shot learning calculates a joint local and global asymmetric measure between two multivariate local distributions of queries and classes.
A task-aware Contrastive Measure Strategy (CMS) is proposed to further enhance the measure function.
On miniImageNet, the ADM network achieves a 3.02% gain over the state-of-the-art method on the 5-way 1-shot task.
On tieredImageNet, the ADM network achieves a 1.56% gain over the state-of-the-art method on the 5-way 1-shot task.

claim_records.text: RankDNN casts relevance ranking for image retrieval as binary ranking relation classification.
RankDNN's core component is a simple MLP that takes an image triplet encoded as the difference between two vector-Kronecker products and outputs a binary relevance ranking order.
During meta test, RankDNN ranks support images according to their similarity with query samples, and each query sample is assigned the class label of its nearest neighbor.
RankDNN effectively improves the performance of its baselines based on a variety of backbones.
RankDNN outperforms previous state-of-the-art algorithms on multiple few-shot learning benchmarks including miniImageNet, tieredImageNet, Caltech-UCSD Birds, and CIFAR-FS.
Experiments on the cross-domain challenge demonstrate the superior transferability of RankDNN.
RankDNN can be flexibly fused with other post-processing methods.

claim_records.text: DeepEMD employs the Earth Mover's Distance (EMD) as a metric to compute a structural distance between dense image representations to determine image relevance.
The EMD generates optimal matching flows between structural elements that have the minimum matching cost, which is used to calculate the image distance for classification.

DeepEMD designs a cross-reference mechanism to generate important weights of elements in the EMD formulation, which can effectively alleviate the adverse impact caused by cluttered background and large intra-class appearance variations.
To implement k-shot classification, DeepEMD proposes to learn a structured fully connected layer that can directly classify dense image representations with the EMD.
Based on the implicit function theorem, the EMD can be inserted as a layer into the network for end-to-end training.

DeepEMD outperforms state-of-the-art methods by a significant margin on five widely used few-shot classification benchmarks: miniImageNet, tieredImageNet, Fewshot-CIFAR100 (FC100), Caltech-UCSD Birds-200-2011 (CUB), and CIFAR-FewShot (CIFAR-FS).
DeepEMD demonstrates effectiveness on the image retrieval task in its experiments.

claim_records.text: The proposed QSFormer model involves a global query-support sample Transformer (sampleFormer) branch and a local patch Transformer (patchFormer) learning branch.
The sampleFormer branch adopts Encoder, Decoder and Cross-Attention to respectively model Support representation, Query image representation and metric learning for the few-shot classification task.

The local patch Transformer extracts structural representation for each image sample by capturing the long-range dependence of local image patches, serving as a complement to the global learning branch.
A novel Cross-scale Interactive Feature Extractor (CIFE) is proposed to extract and fuse multi-scale CNN features as an effective backbone module for the few-shot learning method.
All modules of the QSFormer framework are integrated into a unified framework and trained in an end-to-end manner.
Extensive experiments on four popular datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of the proposed QSFormer.
